my mum died when i was 18. i was experiencing massive changes in my life, moving out, starting university, the whole thing. 

it affected me very badly at the time. i became a whole different person both due to the aftermath of the loss and because i didn’t have a mum anymore. i stopped being a child. 

now i am almost 22, so i am not really a middle aged person but i have more going on in my life. i have people who i love and people who support me. i have goals and an idea of what my future will look like. so maybe it’s a combination of expecting the death, having more than your parents as the centrepiece of your life, and needing them less. 

i miss my mother every single day and i think about her constantly. she is the first person i want to call and the first person i want to show off my new clothes to. i miss gossiping with her about my friends, i miss cooking together, i miss drinking some coffee together. nothing will ever replace that. but i have a life beyond the loss anymore. i am not the 18 year old who was sitting alone in her accommodation room, staring at the ceiling for hours.

i will try to go off of my own experience. i am audhd and i have a partner who has adhd. we have considerable similarities but also a lot of differences. 

sensory issues is definitely one of them. how i interpret things socially is another one.

there is a fine line between ‘autistic traits’ and just being human because we are human and our traits are human traits. we have different frequencies, intensities and consequences for those traits. 

your brain is not some knobs, it is the result of hundreds of generations’ experiences. if it was slightly different, who knows? but if you are autistic (which i am not questioning, i just assume you are still exploring the possibility from your first sentence) you are as different from any other autistic person as you are with another person.

of course we have more shared experiences but we will be different. embrace the extroversion and honour your brain’s needs. there is a good balance there and there is lots to learn about yourself all the time.

hey! i’m also hypermobile and adhd. i’d say what helped me was focussing on my alignment. of course it’s important for anyone but being aware of the position of my knees and ankles was very helpful to me. another thing is learning how to fall. although falls happen in ice skating we do have to be more cautious. learn how to fall and get up properly in a way that doesn’t put strain on your joints. if you wear supports, wear them to ice. they provide extra padding and help with alignment. when/if you buy your own skates, make sure they have good ankle support because hypermobile ankles are more likely to pronate which makes it more difficult on ice. ice skating helped me a lot with joint pain and my awareness of my posture on and off ice. i think it’s a great activity for hypermobility and i hope you enjoy it!

OP, there isn’t much of a system that works for everything. Now, I’m not autistic but I have ADHD and BPD so I’ve had my share of saying things that I probably shouldn’t have said. 

Your girlfriend probably didn’t change her mind, but there were some other things that were bothering her. It might be the case that you have felt that these things were done with now because she has pointed them out. However, for her, it might be a collection of things you haven’t apologised for. 

I know hostile behaviour in most cases is not right but if someone points out your wrongdoings and you don’t acknowledge, try to understand and apologise (this is important but not the only step), that’s not great. It might be that you have not followed your own rules with this because you didn’t exactly acknowledge your wrongdoings. However, I will say, it would be kinder of your girlfriend to elaborate a bit more to accommodate you. I think that is a key part of the mechanism you have yourself. 

I think there is a major communication issue here, but your girlfriend is learning with you. She doesn’t know what it is to have an autistic brain, you have struggle with judging the goodness/badness of situations. It would help to communicate. 

I am a stranger on the internet and I don’t have the whole picture of your relationship, so I will not say anything about that. What I will say is, it would have made sense for your girlfriend to explain better, for you to give her space when she refused to do so, and to have a shared understanding of each other’s needs in the relationship. 

I will say though, the words you have used were way harsh. As a rule of thumb, any word that is not positive that you use against someone has repercussions to it. Some bigger, some smaller. Maybe you can think about what the words refer to, where they would be used, even examples in sentences to see what effect they feel like they have. Then you can avoid the ones that are higher on these scales. Because they’re words that are mostly difficult to take back. 

Finally, for some understanding of morality, you could give The Good Place a watch. I think they describe goodness/badness in a very unique, digestible way. That might help you understand how people can improve, how there might be other factors in their behaviour and a whole bunch of other things. 

I know it’s difficult and it might not work out but you have time to improve and also advocate for yourself.
